items.text: You already know what a shader is: a function the GPU runs a huge number of times at once. But knowing what it is does not tell you how to make one. What does that function receive? What does it have to return? Who calls it, and with what data?

sentences.text: You already know what a shader is:
a function the GPU runs a huge number of times at once.
But knowing what it is does not tell you how to make one.
What does that function receive?
What does it have to return?
Who calls it, and with what data?

items.text: In this chapter you will not write code or install anything. You will follow the complete journey of a drawing, from your game to the screen, one step after another. Take your time with it, because everything you write later in C# is one of these steps. If you understand the journey, the code explains itself.

items.text: 5. The spreading: from three values to thousands

items.text: Something happens here that is almost never explained, and it is the key to understanding everything else.

sentences.text: Something happens here that is almost never explained, and it is the key to understanding everything else.

items.text: The Vertex function returned three colors, one per vertex. But the triangle has thousands of pixels. Which color reaches each one?

But the triangle has thousands of pixels.

items.text: The GPU spreads them. It gives each pixel a mix of the three values, depending on how close it is to each vertex:

sentences.text: The GPU spreads them.
It gives each pixel a mix of the three values, depending on how close it is to each vertex:

items.text: A pixel right next to the red vertex receives almost all red.

items.text: What the Vertex function returns is not what the Fragment function receives. Vertex returns three exact values, one per vertex. Fragment receives thousands, one per pixel, and each one is a different mix. The data has the same name on both sides, but on the way the GPU spread it.

sentences.text: What the Vertex function returns is not what the Fragment function receives.
Vertex returns three exact values, one per vertex.
Fragment receives thousands, one per pixel, and each one is a different mix.
The data has the same name on both sides, but on the way the GPU spread it.

items.text: 7. The slots: how each stage knows which data is which

sentences.text: 7. The slots: how each stage knows which data is which

items.text: So far we talked about "the position" and "the color", by name. But the GPU does not understand names. For it the data travels in numbered slots.

sentences.text: So far we talked about "the position" and "the color", by name.
But the GPU does not understand names.
For it the data travels in numbered slots.

items.text: Your game says: "I put the position in slot 0 and the color in slot 1". And the Vertex function says: "I read the position from slot 0 and the color from slot 1". They understand each other by the number.

sentences.text: Your game says:
"I put the position in slot 0 and the color in slot 1".
And the Vertex function says:
"I read the position from slot 0 and the color from slot 1".
They understand each other by the number.

items.text: That number is called a location.

sentences.text: That number is called a location.

items.text: Which number goes with which data is up to you. Slot 0 is not the position by rule: you could put the color in slot 0 and the position in slot 1, as long as your game does the same. The GPU only sees the number and the type: slot 0, two floats; slot 1, four floats. Each slot holds up to four numbers, and every GPU offers at least 16 of them for the vertex data. If you get a number wrong no error appears: the shader reads the wrong data and the drawing comes out wrong.

items.text: The number between brackets, location, is how GLSL names a slot. GLSL is the language of OpenGL and Vulkan. HLSL, the language of DirectX, names the same thing with a word and an index, such as TEXCOORD0. Metal, WebGPU and SPIR-V have their own words too. So which one do you write? The one you already know. Yotsuba Shader has five styles: GLSL, HLSL, MSL (Metal), WGSL (WebGPU) and SPIR-V. Only the words of the interface change; the math and the C# stay exactly the same. Use the Style dropdown at the top right of this page to see every example in the style you prefer.

items.text: This table works like a small dictionary between the five styles. Each row is one idea, and each column is how one style says it. A channel of vertex data is location in GLSL and WGSL, TEXCOORD in HLSL, attribute in Metal, and Location with a capital L in SPIR-V. The final position is gl_Position in GLSL, SV_Position in HLSL, position in Metal, and so on. And where the color goes is location zero in most of them, and SV_Target in HLSL. The words are different, but for the compiler they are the same idea.

items.text: There is one difference worth knowing. With a number such as location(0) you choose the number. With a semantic such as TEXCOORD, the compiler can choose the number for you, and it connects the two stages by the name: the TEXCOORD(0) that leaves Vertex is the one Fragment receives. The final result is the same kind of slot.

It copies the position and the color.

items.text: This table sums up the whole journey, one row per decision. In the first row, each vertex carries its position in slot zero and its color in slot one. In the second, what Vertex hands to Fragment is the final position, which is the special one, and the color in slot zero. The third says the Vertex function only copies the position and the color. The fourth, that Fragment returns the color it receives. And the fifth, that this color leaves through slot zero.

items.text: We also compiled the same shader written in each of the five styles: the GLSL, GLSL ES, Metal and C++ files come out identical, character by character. HLSL and SPIR-V keep the names you wrote, so in those two the only differences are the names you chose, for example the "TEXCOORD0" that SPIR-V remembers in a UserSemantic line when you write in the HLSL style.

items.text: The compiler turns your C# into SPIR-V first, and from there it generates the other languages. That is why a name like TEXCOORD and a number like location(0) can mean the same thing for it: both end up as the same slot in SPIR-V.
